content:
Arthritis doesn't have to stop you travelling. With proper planning, you can enjoy holidays in the UK and abroad. This guide covers everything from travel insurance to managing medications while away.

Quick answer: When travelling with arthritis, declare your condition for travel insurance and carry medications in hand luggage with a GP letter. Request airport assistance, reserve an aisle seat, and move frequently during flights. Choose accessible accommodation, such as ground-floor rooms or those with lifts and walk-in showers. Pace yourself, use a fold-up walking stick, and consider a RADAR key for accessible toilets.

Before You Go

Travel Insurance

Standard travel insurance may not cover pre-existing conditions like arthritis. You need to:

  • Declare arthritis when buying travel insurance
  • Specialist providers: AllClear, InsureWith, Avanti, Staysure
  • Cover should include emergency treatment for flare-ups abroad
  • GHIC (Global Health Insurance Card) provides access to state healthcare in EU countries — apply free at nhs.uk

Medications

  • Carry medications in original packaging with prescription labels
  • Take enough for your trip plus a few extra days
  • Keep medications in hand luggage (never checked luggage)
  • Carry a letter from your GP listing your medications — especially for controlled drugs or injectable biologics
  • Check destination country rules on medication imports

Flying with Arthritis

  • Request assistance — airports provide free assistance from check-in to the gate (book 48 hours ahead)
  • Aisle seat — easier to get up and move during the flight
  • Move regularly — walk the aisle every 30-60 minutes to prevent stiffness
  • Compression socks — reduce swelling on long flights
  • Support pillows — neck and lumbar pillows for comfort
  • Stay hydrated — cabin air is very dry
  • Time medication — adjust for time zones on long-haul flights

Accessible Accommodation

  • Look for ground-floor rooms or properties with lifts
  • Check for walk-in showers (no bath step-over)
  • UK: search "accessible holiday cottages" on DisabledHolidays.com or AccessAble
  • Hotels: Travelodge accessible rooms are reliably equipped
  • Cruise ships: often excellent for accessibility

UK Accessible Breaks

  • Calvert Trust — accessible activity holidays in Exmoor, Lake District, Kielder
  • Center Parcs — adapted lodges and accessible facilities
  • National Trust — many properties have accessibility guides on their website
  • Seaside towns — many have beach wheelchairs available

During Your Trip

  • Pace yourself — don't try to pack every day full of activities
  • Build in rest days
  • Carry a fold-up walking stick or portable seat for queues
  • Apply for a RADAR key (£5 from Disability Rights UK) — opens 10,000+ accessible toilets across the UK
  • Keep a cool bag for biologic medications if they need refrigeration

Don't let arthritis stop you exploring. With the right preparation, you can travel comfortably and create wonderful memories.

Practical next steps for Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide

If you came here about Travelling with Arthritis – UK & Abroad Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Travelling with Arthritis Abroad

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
